title: How Do Bees Make Honey?
question: How do bees make honey?
answer: Bees sip watery nectar from flowers and carry it home in a special honey stomach. Enzymes start to change it. Then bees dry it with tiny bubbles, warmth and wing-fanning until it is thick and sweet. Last, they seal it in wax cells to keep as food.

visual.what: A sunny kitchen table with a jar of golden honey. Bối holds the jar up and looks puzzled, Beo peeks over the table, and Huy and Hùng smile beside them.

parts.text: Huy, this honey came from bees. But bees are so tiny! How do they make something this sweet and sticky?
Great question, Bối. And here is a surprise. To make honey, bees blow bubbles. Lots and lots of tiny bubbles.
Bees blowing bubbles? Like me in the bath!

visual.what: Huy talks to the camera with a cartoon honey bee buzzing around his head, while the other three wave in the background.

parts.text: Today we will find out where honey really starts, what happens inside a bee, and how bees turn a runny drink into thick, golden honey. Let's fly!

visual.what: A garden with flowers. Bối points at a flower and pretends to scoop with a tiny spoon, while Huy kneels beside her.

parts.text: I know! Flowers have honey inside, and bees just scoop it up and carry it home.
That is a really good guess, and you are partly right. Bees do start with flowers. But flowers do not hold honey. They hold nectar. Nectar is a sweet, watery juice, much runnier than honey.

visual.what: Hùng holds a glass of runny water in one hand and a jar of thick honey in the other. The water is labelled like nectar, runny, and the honey is labelled honey, thick.

parts.text: Look. Nectar is runny, like this water. Honey is thick, like this. Totally different!
So something must happen to the nectar to turn it into honey. That is the part we need to find out.

visual.what: Beo looks up at Huy with a worried face, and a little thought bubble shows a bee with a question mark. Bối giggles behind her hand.

parts.text: Wait. Is honey bee poop?
Lots of kids wonder that! No, it is not. Bees have a special pouch just for carrying nectar. It is separate from the stomach that digests the bee's own food. Let's see how it all works.

visual.what: A simple map with a beehive in the middle and a dotted circle around it labelled about 3 km. A bee flies from the hive to a patch of flowers inside the circle.

parts.text: Step one. It all starts with a forager bee. A forager is a bee whose job is to go out and find food. It flies to nearby flowers, usually no more than about 3 kilometres from home.

visual.what: A big friendly bee on a flower, with its long tongue labelled proboscis dipping into the flower like a drinking straw.

parts.text: The bee has a long tongue called a proboscis. Say it with me. Pro-BOSS-is. It works like a drinking straw, and the bee uses it to suck up the nectar.
A built-in straw! I want one for my juice.

visual.what: A see-through cartoon bee. A small pouch labelled honey stomach sits just above a second pouch labelled food stomach, with a little lunch box icon next to the honey stomach.

parts.text: The nectar goes into the bee's honey stomach, also called the honey crop. It sits just above the bee's food stomach. Think of it as a lunch box inside the bee, used to carry nectar home.
My lunch box has a sandwich in it.

visual.what: A counter clicking up to 1,000 as a bee zips from flower to flower across a big meadow, with a small clock showing more than one hour.

parts.text: The honey stomach is small. To fill it, a bee may visit more than a thousand flowers. That can take more than an hour of nonstop work.
A thousand flowers for one tummy full? Wow!

visual.what: On the left, a bee with a full, round honey stomach. On the right, Hùng wobbling under a giant backpack stuffed with pillows, legs bending.

parts.text: When it is full, the nectar weighs about half as much as the bee itself. Imagine flying home with a backpack half as heavy as you!
Whoa, whoa! I can't even walk with this, never mind fly!
So, step one. A bee sips watery nectar and carries it home in its honey stomach.

visual.what: Zooming in on a bee's head. Tiny glowing dots labelled enzymes flow from small glands near the mouth into the nectar.

parts.text: Step two. Something clever happens inside the bee. The bee adds enzymes to the nectar. Enzymes are tiny helpers made by the body. These come from glands near the bee's mouth, a bit like special spit.

visual.what: Hùng holds a long paper chain labelled big sugar and snips it with round-tipped scissors into short pieces labelled small sugars, next to cartoon enzyme scissors doing the same.

parts.text: The enzymes work like tiny scissors. They cut big sugars into smaller, simpler sugars. This is the start of turning nectar into honey.
One big sugar, snip, snip, lots of little sugars!

visual.what: Inside a cosy hive, a forager bee passes a drop of nectar mouth to mouth to a hive bee. Bối laughs and Beo makes a funny face.

parts.text: Back at the hive, the forager passes the nectar to a hive bee, mouth to mouth. A hive bee is a bee whose job is to work inside the hive.
Mouth to mouth? That is like sharing a smoothie the weird way!
Eww! But cool.
A bit weird for us, but perfect for bees. And the hive bee adds even more enzymes.

visual.what: Huy holds up a card with a drop of nectar and a little enzyme helper on it.

parts.text: Step two takeaway. Inside the bees, enzymes start changing nectar into something new.

visual.what: A close-up of a hive bee holding a shiny little bubble of nectar between its jaws, with arrows showing it going out and back in.

parts.text: Step three. Remember the bubbles? Here they are. The hive bee pushes out a little drop of nectar and holds it between its jaws, making a tiny bubble. Then it sucks it back in. Again and again.
The bees really do blow bubbles!

visual.what: On the left, a deep cup of water with only a small top touching the air. On the right, the same water spread as a wide flat puddle with many little steam wisps rising.

parts.text: Why bubbles? A bubble spreads the nectar out thin, so lots of it touches the warm air. Then water escapes into the air faster. It is like a puddle, which dries faster when it is spread out flat.

visual.what: A line of bees passing a nectar drop from one to the next like a relay baton, with arrows between them and a small timer showing up to 20 minutes.

parts.text: Bees work in teams, like a relay race. One bee bubbles the nectar, then passes it on to the next. This can go on for up to 20 minutes.
Like my race at school!

visual.what: Hùng holds a big cardboard honeycomb model. Labels point to beeswax, a cell, and the six-sided shape called a hexagon.

parts.text: Then the bees put the new honey into the honeycomb. Honeycomb is made of beeswax, a wax that bees make. It has hundreds or thousands of little rooms called cells. Each cell has six sides. That shape is called a hexagon.
Count them with me. One, two, three, four, five, six sides!

visual.what: Bees on a honeycomb beat their wings, with wavy arrows carrying water drops out of the hive and a thermometer showing about 35 °C. Hùng waves a paper fan so hard his hair blows up.

parts.text: But this honey is still too watery. So the bees keep the honey area warm, about 35 degrees Celsius, as warm as a hot summer day. And they beat their wings together, moving air over the honey to carry the water away.
Bee fans! Whoosh!
Whoosh! Oops, I fanned my own hair up.

visual.what: Two jars side by side. The nectar jar is filled about three quarters with blue water, and the honey jar has only about one fifth blue water and the rest golden.

parts.text: Nectar starts out about three quarters water. Finished honey is only about one fifth water. That is why honey is so thick.
Step three takeaway. Bees dry the nectar with bubbles, warmth and fanning until it becomes thick honey.

visual.what: A row of honeycomb cells full of golden honey, with bees pressing flat wax lids on top. One lid is labelled wax lid.

parts.text: Step four. When the honey is ready, the bees seal each cell with a lid of wax. The lid keeps dirt out and stops the honey from drying any more.

visual.what: Zooming into a drop of honey. Tiny cartoon germs bounce off it with sad faces, unable to get in.

parts.text: Honey has so much sugar and so little water that most germs cannot grow in it. Germs are tiny living things, too small to see. So honey that is stored well does not go bad.
The germs can't come in?
Some germs may get in, but most of them can't grow in it. Honey is a tough little fortress.

visual.what: A timeline stretching back thousands of years, with an archaeologist holding up an old clay pot at the far end and a modern closed honey jar at today's end.

parts.text: Scientists think honey can last for thousands of years. They say some very old honey found by archaeologists was still safe to eat, but not everyone agrees about the oldest finds. Archaeologists are people who dig up old things to learn about the past. Honey must also be kept in a closed jar. If it soaks up water from damp air, it can spoil.
Thousands of years? That is older than Grandpa!

visual.what: A snowy winter outside a hive. Inside, bees huddle together eating honey from the comb, and small baby bees called larvae lie in their cells.

parts.text: Why do bees work so hard? Honey is their food store. They eat it when it is cold or when food is hard to find. They also feed it to their babies, called larvae. Honey has much more energy than nectar, so it is a super snack.

visual.what: A beekeeper in a white bee suit and veil lifts a honeycomb frame from a wooden hive, while Huy and the kids watch from far away behind a fence.

parts.text: Beekeepers are people who look after bees. They take some of the extra honey. Good beekeepers make sure the bees keep enough food for winter.
And remember, never poke or touch a beehive. Leave hives to beekeepers in their special suits.

visual.what: Huy holds up a sealed honeycomb piece with a snowflake sticker on it.

parts.text: Step four takeaway. Bees seal the honey in wax and save it as food for hard times.

visual.what: Bối dressed in a cardboard bee costume with antennas, flopping onto a big flower like a bed, surrounded by many flowers.

parts.text: Imagine if you were a bee! To fill your honey stomach, you would visit more than a thousand flowers. Then you would fly home carrying a load half as heavy as you.
I would need a really long nap after that!

visual.what: Hùng sets two wet paper towels on a table, one laid flat and one squashed into a ball. A drip lands on his sock and he hops.

parts.text: Here is a safe test to try at home. Ask a grown-up for two paper towels and wet them both. Leave one flat and squash the other into a ball. Which one will dry first?
Oops, my sock got wet first!
The flat one, because more of it touches the air. Just like the bee bubbles!
Exactly. Spreading out helps water escape.

visual.what: Hùng tilts a plate with a spoon of water racing down one side and a spoon of honey creeping slowly on the other. Beo watches closely, chin on the table.

parts.text: One more. With a grown-up, tip a spoon of water and a spoon of honey onto a tilted plate. The water races away. The honey crawls slowly, because the bees took most of the water out.
Honey is a snail!

visual.what: A loop of four pictures joined by arrows. A bee sipping a flower, enzyme scissors, a bee blowing a bubble with wings fanning, and a sealed wax cell.

parts.text: So how do bees make honey? They sip watery nectar from flowers and carry it home in their honey stomachs. Enzymes start to change it. Then bees dry it with bubbles, warmth and fanning until it is thick and sweet, and seal it in wax.

visual.what: A balance scale with a beehive and a pile of honey jars labelled about 29 kg on one side and Bối on the other side, level.

parts.text: And here is a fun fact. One hive can make about 29 kilograms of honey in a year. That is about as heavy as a nine year old child!
That is a lot of bubbles!

visual.what: All four wave at the camera. A bee flies toward a hive with a question mark over it, and a big button reads Subscribe to Ask Huy.

parts.text: Next time we will ask, how do bees find their way back home? Subscribe to Ask Huy so you do not miss it!
Bye bye!
Buzz buzz!

facts.claim: Honey is made by honeybees from nectar, the sweet juice from flowers.
Nectar is much runnier than finished honey.
Nectar goes to a honey stomach (honey crop), which sits above and is separate from the food stomach that digests the bee's own food.
Foraging bees collect nectar and bring it back to the hive.
Bees usually do not go more than about two miles (about 3 km) from the hive for nectar.
Bees suck up nectar through a proboscis.
Filling the honey stomach can take visits to more than a thousand flowers and more than an hour of nonstop work.
A full honey stomach holds about 40 mg, about half the weight of an unladen bee.
Enzymes from a gland of the bee are added to the nectar and break complex sugars into simpler sugars like glucose and fructose.
Foragers pass nectar mouth to mouth to hive bees at the hive.
Hive bees repeatedly form nectar bubbles between their jaws; the large surface area helps water evaporate into the warm hive air.
Hive bees work in relay groups, and processing can take up to about 20 minutes.
Honeycomb is made of beeswax and has hundreds or thousands of six-sided (hexagonal) cells where honey is stored.
Honey storage areas are kept at about 35 °C, and bees fan their wings to move air over the honey and remove water.
Nectar is about 70 to 80% water; finished honey is about 18% water or less.
Bees cap finished honey cells with wax, sealing them from contamination and stopping further evaporation.
Because of its high sugar content most microorganisms cannot grow in honey, so stored honey does not spoil.
Old honey found by archaeologists has been reported edible after thousands of years, but claims about edible honey from Egyptian tombs have been disputed.
Honey exposed to moist air pulls in water and can begin to ferment.
Bees eat stored honey in cold weather or when food is scarce, feed it to their larvae, and honey has much more energy than nectar.
Beekeepers harvest honey and make sure bees have enough food to survive the winter.
On average a hive produces about 29 kg of honey per year.
Spread-out water dries faster than bunched-up water because more of it touches the air.

description: How do tiny bees turn flower juice into thick, golden honey? Join Huy, his helper Hùng, Bối and little Beo as they follow nectar from the flower into a bee's honey stomach and through the hive, where bees blow bubbles and fan their wings to make honey. A calm, fact-checked science adventure for kids aged 6 to 12, with two safe experiments to try at home with a grown-up.

cast.name: Huy
cast.role: the host (25): curious, warm, a little funny; explains

cast.name: Hùng
cast.role: Huy's younger brother (21), his hands-on assistant: sets up and runs the experiments and demos, brings things, now and then a funny little mishap

cast.name: Bối
cast.role: an 8-year-old girl who asks, guesses and tries things

cast.name: Beo
cast.role: Bối's 5-year-old little brother: curious, makes funny innocent guesses
